posts.excerpt: A good marathon plan is not magic. It moves through four phases: base, development, sharpening and taper. Here is how to build one around your life.

author.name: Alex
author.bio: Developer & runner. Went from 3:01 to 2:06 in the half marathon.

posts.content:
# How to Build a Training Plan for Your Goal Race (Without Guessing)

For my first two years of running, I had no training plan. I just ran as much as felt right. In practice, that meant switching between "not enough" and "too much, and then injured."

When I finally followed a proper plan for the half marathon, I took 20 minutes off my time in a single training block. That did not happen because I ran more. I had been running *more* for years. It happened because I ran the right sessions, in the right order, at the right time.

Here is what I learned about building a plan that actually works.

## The Four-Phase Model

Almost every serious training plan follows the same four phases, whatever the race distance:

### 1. Base Building (40% of your training)
This phase builds your aerobic base — your body's ability to use oxygen over a long time. It is nearly all easy running, plus perhaps one faster tempo run each week. The goal is not to get fast yet. The goal is to prepare your body so that it can get fast later: more small blood vessels in your muscles, more energy factories inside your muscle cells, and stronger tendons and ligaments.

Base miles are boring. Run them anyway.

### 2. Development (30% of your training)
Now you start to add structure: moderate tempo runs, long runs with some marathon-pace running, and progression runs that get faster near the end. You are teaching your body to deal with lactate (a by-product of hard effort) at higher speeds.

This is where most amateur runners start. That is why most amateur runners stop improving.

### 3. Sharpening (25% of your training)
Now the hard work begins: VO2max intervals (short, fast repeats), race-pace runs, and tune-up races. Your aerobic base lets you absorb these hard sessions without breaking down — because you built it first.

Without the base phase, this is where runners get injured. With it, this is where runners get fast.

### 4. Taper (5-10% of your training)
Your weekly distance drops by 30-50%. The intensity stays. Your body finally takes in all the training from the previous 10-16 weeks, and you arrive at the start line fresh.

The taper is not a rest period. It is a precise, planned phase.

## How Long Should Your Plan Be?

That depends on your goal race and your current fitness:

| Race | Beginner | Intermediate | Advanced |
|------|----------|--------------|----------|
| 5K | 8 weeks | 10 weeks | 12 weeks |
| 10K | 10 weeks | 12 weeks | 14 weeks |
| Half Marathon | 12 weeks | 14 weeks | 16 weeks |
| Marathon | 16 weeks | 18 weeks | 20 weeks |

If your goal race is 8 weeks away and you have not started training, you are not too late. You simply have a shorter block. Adjust your expectations, and still follow the same phase structure inside the time you have.

## The Biggest Mistake: Running All Runs at the Same Pace

This is where most self-coached runners go wrong. They have no clear easy days and hard days. Every run is a medium effort, and a medium effort gives medium results.

The research is clear: for most recreational runners, 80% of your weekly distance should be easy. Truly easy. Easy enough to hold a conversation, feel slightly bored, and wonder whether you are working hard enough.

You are. The benefits of easy running build up slowly. They keep building while you sleep and while you sit at your desk, for about 48 hours after the run. All that easy running is quietly upgrading your engine.

The other 20% is where you earn race fitness: tempo runs, intervals, and long runs with some race-pace work.

## What Paces Should You Train At?

This is where VDOT helps. VDOT is a single number that describes your current running fitness. Enter a recent race result into the [VDOT Calculator](/vdot) and you get exact paces for each training zone:

- **Easy pace**: you can talk in full sentences
- **Marathon pace**: hard, but under control
- **Threshold pace**: comfortably uncomfortable
- **Interval pace**: hard, but not a sprint
- **Repetition pace**: fast

These are not rough suggestions. They come directly from your current fitness. Running faster than your easy pace on easy days does not make you fitter. It only makes you more tired.

## Building Around Your Life

The best training plan is the one you will actually follow. Before you build the weeks, answer these questions:

**Which days can you run reliably?** Most plans assume 4-5 days per week. If you can only manage 4, that is fine. Drop the recovery run, and keep the long run and the two quality sessions.

**How much time do you have on the weekend?** The long run is the most important session in every plan. Protect Saturday or Sunday, and treat the other day as secondary.

**When is your main race?** Count backwards from race day and build your phases from there. Race day is week N. The taper starts at N-2 (for a 5K or 10K) or N-3 (for a half or full marathon). Sharpening fills the weeks before that.

## The Free Training Plan Generator

I built [TrainPace's Training Plan Generator](/plan) to do exactly this work for you. You tell it:
- Your goal race (5K, 10K, Half, Marathon)
- Your race date
- The days you can train
- Your current fitness level
- Your goal time (optional)

It then creates a complete plan with all four phases — week by week, workout by workout — with paces based on Jack Daniels' VDOT method. If you have already worked out your VDOT on the [VDOT Calculator](/vdot), your training paces carry over automatically.

You can also export the full plan to your calendar as an .ics file, which imports straight into Google Calendar or Apple Calendar. Every workout lands on the right date, with the duration, the description and the pace zone included.

## The Most Important Principle

Consistency beats everything else.

A 14-week plan where you complete 85% of the workouts will beat a 20-week plan where you complete 60%. Regular easy mileage, repeated week after week, is what drives improvement — not the occasional heroic long run.

Do not skip the easy days because they feel too easy. Do not skip the hard days because they sound frightening. Turn up, do the session in front of you, and trust the process.

The plan works if you do the plan.

posts.title: How to Pace a Marathon: The Complete Strategy Guide
posts.excerpt: Most marathons are lost in the first 10km, not the last. Here is how to pace one from start to finish: your splits, your effort, and what to do when it hurts.

author.name: Alex
author.bio: Developer & runner. Went from 3:01 to 2:06 in the half marathon.

posts.content:
# How to Pace a Marathon: The Complete Strategy Guide

The marathon is the only race where the most dangerous moment is the first one. Start 10 seconds per kilometer too fast and you will pay for it from kilometer 30 onward. Get it right and you will pass 30 runners in the last 5 kilometers.

This guide is about getting it right.

## The Two Mistakes That Ruin Marathons

### 1. Starting Too Fast

Think about your last race. Did you feel great at halfway? And how did you feel at 35 km? The difference between those two feelings usually depends on how fast you ran the first 10 km.

The crowd is loud at the start. Your legs feel fresh. Your training is finished. Everything tells you to go. And if you go, you will pay for it.

The "wall" at 30–35 km happens when you run out of stored carbohydrate (glycogen). Early pace mistakes make that happen sooner. Running 15 seconds per kilometer too fast in the first half burns your glycogen more quickly and leaves you empty at exactly the moment you need the most.

### 2. Running by Feel Instead of Target Pace

In the first 10 km of a marathon, your correct target pace feels easy. Strangely, almost worryingly easy. Runners who have never felt this ignore the GPS watch and run by feel, and they end up running too fast.

That is why you need a plan before race day.

## Even Split vs. Negative Split

There are two standard ways to pace a marathon:

**Even split**: the same pace for every kilometer of the 42.195 km. This takes a lot of discipline in the first half, and it usually gives the most reliable results for recreational runners.

**Negative split**: run the second half faster than the first. The best marathon times are usually run with a small negative split (1–2 minutes faster in the second half). For recreational runners, aiming for an even pace often produces a natural negative split anyway, because most people start carefully.

For most runners, **aiming for even splits and finishing with a small negative split** is the best strategy.

## How to Calculate Your Target Pace

Start with your goal finish time. Use the [pace calculator](/calculator) to find your exact split per kilometer or mile.

For a 3:30:00 marathon:
- Target pace: 4:58/km (7:59/mile)
- First half: 1:45:00
- Second half: 1:44:30–1:45:00 (the same or slightly faster)

Write these splits on your wrist, set pace alerts on your watch, and stay with them for the first 25 km, however you feel.

## The Boston Qualifier Rule of Thumb

If you are chasing a big personal best, there is a simple rule: **if you feel comfortable, you are running correctly**. If you feel great at 20 km, something is wrong. If you feel in control — working, but under control — you are on target.

For most runners the discomfort arrives at about 28–32 km. If it comes earlier, you started too fast. If it never comes, you had more to give.

## Splits by Phase

### Kilometers 1–10: Be Conservative

Your body is warming up. Your glycogen stores are full. Your legs feel bouncy. This is when the race feels easiest, and it is when most of the damage is done.

Run 5–10 seconds per kilometer **slower** than target pace. If your goal is 5:00/km, run 5:05–5:10. You get that time back in the second half, when other runners slow down.

### Kilometers 10–25: Settle In

This is your cruising phase. Find your rhythm. Hit your target pace again and again. Do not react to runners passing you or to the crowd. Just follow the plan.

### Kilometers 25–35: The Test

This is where the race really starts. Your glycogen is running low. Your legs are getting heavy. Every kilometer feels like an argument with yourself.

Now think about effort rather than pace. Keep the same **effort level** you have had since kilometer 10. Your pace may drop a little, and that is fine. What matters is keeping the effort honest.

This is also when fueling mistakes catch up with you. If you have not taken in enough carbohydrate all race, you will find out at about kilometer 30.

### Kilometers 35–42.195: Everything You Have

Pace does not matter now. Only moving forward matters. Shorten your stride if your form starts to fall apart. Run the tangents. Count to 100. Focus on the next runner ahead. Do whatever gets you to the finish line.

If you have paced the race well, your last 7 km will be among the fastest you run all day.

## Weather Adjustments

Hot, humid weather means you must slow down. A simple guide:
- Above 16°C: add 5–10 seconds/km
- Above 20°C: add 15–20 seconds/km
- Above 24°C: add 30+ seconds/km, or change your goal quite a lot

Ignoring the weather is a common reason runners fall apart late in a race.

## The Fueling Connection

Pacing and fueling go together. Even a perfect pacing plan can fall apart if you do not take in enough carbohydrate. For most marathons:

- Start fueling at kilometer 5 (earlier than you think you need to)
- Aim for 40–60 g of carbohydrate per hour
- Take gels or chews at fixed times, not when you feel you need them (by then it is too late)

Use the [Fuel Planner](/fuel) to work out how many gels to carry, when to take them, and which aid stations to use.

## Race Day Checklist

**The night before:**
- Know your target pace per km and your total split times
- Set the pace alerts on your GPS watch
- Check your fueling plan (how many gels, and when)

**Race morning:**
- Do not start faster than target pace, even if you feel great
- Run the tangents (stay on the inside of curves) — this saves 100–200 meters
- Start drinking before you feel thirsty

**When it gets hard (it will):**
- Shorten your stride before you let your step rate drop
- Focus on keeping good form, not on holding pace
- Remember: everyone is suffering at kilometer 35

## Using the Pace Calculator Before Race Day

The best tool I know for race preparation is the [pace calculator](/calculator). Enter your goal time, get your target pace per kilometer, and write it on your wrist.

If you have a recent race time (5K, 10K or half marathon), you can also use the VDOT race prediction to check whether your marathon goal is realistic. A goal time that is too ambitious is the most common reason marathons go wrong.

posts.title: What is VDOT? The Running Metric That Changes How You Train
posts.excerpt: VDOT is one number that describes your running fitness. It gives you the right pace for every training zone, from easy to interval. Here is how it works.

author.name: Alex
author.bio: Developer & runner. Went from 3:01 to 2:06 in the half marathon.

posts.content:
# What is VDOT? The Running Metric That Changes How You Train

Have you ever wondered why one workout leaves you feeling strong while another leaves you broken, even though the two look similar on paper? The answer is usually pacing. More exactly, running at the wrong intensity for what that session is supposed to do.

VDOT fixes this. It gives you one number that describes your current running fitness, and from that number it works out exact training paces for five different zones. No more guessing. No more running your "easy" run at half-marathon effort and then wondering why your legs are dead on Thursday.

## Where VDOT Comes From

VDOT is an idea from the exercise scientist Jack Daniels, whose book *Daniels' Running Formula* shaped the way distance runners train today. (The capital letters are deliberate. VDOT is not the same as VO2max, although the two are related.)

VO2max is the maximum amount of oxygen your body can use. Measuring it properly needs a lab, a treadmill and a mask. Most runners never have a formal VO2max test.

VDOT skips the lab. It is a number you calculate from a race result. Your time and your distance together give a value that shows your *usable* aerobic fitness: what you can really do in a race. It includes running economy (how efficiently you run) and all the other things that separate a lab number from real performance.

A 50-year-old who trains consistently may have a lower VO2max than a 25-year-old and still beat them in a race, thanks to better economy, better pacing and a stronger head. VDOT captures that. It measures what you do, not what your body should in theory be able to do.

## How to Calculate Your VDOT

All you need is a recent race result, at any distance from 1500 m to the marathon.

Enter your time and distance into the [VDOT Calculator](/vdot). It works out your VDOT score and immediately shows:

- Your **training paces** for each zone (Easy, Marathon, Threshold, Interval, Repetition)
- Your **race predictions** for all the common distances
- Where you rank among runners worldwide, as a **percentage**
- **Example workouts** for each training zone

The calculation uses Daniels' oxygen cost model, an equation, tested against real data, that links running speed to how much oxygen you use.

## The Five Training Zones

VDOT gives you five clear training zones, and each one does a specific job in your body:

### Easy Pace (E)
The foundation zone. Relaxed, conversational running that builds fitness without much stress. Most of your weekly distance belongs here — 70-80% for most runners.

*Purpose:* build your aerobic base, grow the small blood vessels in your muscles and the energy factories inside your muscle cells, help you recover, and improve your running economy.

*Feel:* you can hold a full conversation. Your breathing is steady and relaxed.

### Marathon Pace (M)
The pace you could hold for a whole marathon. A controlled effort, but not a comfortable one.

*Purpose:* teach your body to burn fat at race intensity, and prepare your legs and your mind for marathon effort.

*Feel:* controlled but serious. You can speak in sentences, but you would rather not.

### Threshold Pace (T)
Also called "tempo pace". It is the fastest pace you could hold for about an hour. At this speed, your body clears lactate as fast as it builds up.

*Purpose:* raise the speed you can run at while staying aerobic. This helps your racing at every distance.

*Feel:* "comfortably uncomfortable". You can say a few words, but not a full sentence.

### Interval Pace (I)
VO2max training. You run at your 3K-5K race effort for 3-5 minutes at a time, with the same amount of recovery in between.

*Purpose:* increase the maximum amount of oxygen you can use. Raise the ceiling of your aerobic fitness.

*Feel:* hard. You can say one or two words. Your heart rate is very high.

### Repetition Pace (R)
Short, fast efforts at your mile race pace or faster, with full recovery between them.

*Purpose:* improve your speed and your running economy, and train your muscles and nerves to work together smoothly.

*Feel:* very hard, but short — 30 seconds to 2 minutes per rep, with complete rest.

## Why These Paces Matter More Than Effort

Effort is personal and changeable. A 5/10 effort on a hot, humid Tuesday after a bad night of sleep is not the same, physically, as 5/10 on a cool Saturday morning when you are rested. If you run by feel with nothing to check it against, your paces drift: easy runs get too hard, and hard runs are not hard enough.

VDOT paces are set to what your body can do right now, because they come from a real race result. They match your current fitness — not the fitness you had three months ago, and not the fitness you would like to have, but the fitness you have just proved in a race.

This matters most on easy runs. The VDOT easy pace often surprises runners because it feels *too* slow. That feeling is a sign the system is working. Easy aerobic running does its work below the lactate threshold, so running harder does not speed up the benefits. It only creates more fatigue.

## How VDOT Changes As You Improve

VDOT is not fixed. As you train, race and adapt, it goes up. A VDOT of 40 in January might be 44 by June if you train consistently and race.

When your VDOT rises, all of your training paces get faster too. That is why it is worth re-testing yourself with a tune-up race every 6-8 weeks. If you train at old paces, you either run too slowly (and miss the benefit) or too hard (and collect extra fatigue).

The [VDOT What-If Explorer](/vdot) lets you move the VDOT value up and down and see what the training paces and race predictions would look like at a higher score. It is useful for setting realistic targets.

## VDOT vs. Pace-Based Training

Some coaches set training zones by pace alone: run your easy runs at X:XX/km and your tempo runs at Y:YY/km. That works if those paces match your fitness. The problem is that they often do not, or nobody updates them when your fitness changes.

VDOT solves both problems. The first setting comes from a real race, and updating it only takes a new race result.

Done properly, the two methods end up in the same place. VDOT is simply a clear method for getting the right paces from real data.

## Practical First Steps

1. **Run a race** — even a 5K is enough. A time trial works if you have not raced recently, though an official race is more reliable, because the pressure of the event usually produces a truer effort.

2. **Enter it into the VDOT Calculator** — [trainpace.com/vdot](/vdot). Your score and training paces appear straight away.

3. **Write down your Easy and Threshold paces** — these two will guide 90% of your training.

4. **Build a plan around those paces** — the [Training Plan Generator](/plan) takes your VDOT paces directly if you go there from the VDOT results page.

5. **Test again in 6-8 weeks** — run another race or a proper time trial, then update your numbers.

The first time you look at your VDOT easy pace and realize that you have been running your easy days 90 seconds per kilometer too fast, everything makes sense. The training starts to fit together. The improvement follows.

[Calculate your VDOT →](/vdot)

posts.excerpt: BMO Vancouver Half 2026 race report. The same 2:06, but two very different runners. Why the clock does not tell the truth, and what the heat cost me.

author.name: Alex
author.bio: Developer & runner. Went from 3:01 to 2:06 in the half marathon.

posts.content:
# I Ran the Same Time as Last Year — And It Was a Completely Different Race

**BMO Vancouver Half Marathon 2026 | Race Report**

---

Last year I ran the BMO Vancouver Half Marathon in 2:06:27. This year I ran it in 2:06:08. Same course. Same distance. Almost the same number on the clock.

But it was a completely different race.

## The Goal

Under 2:00. I had spent 12 weeks in a structured training block with my coach. I had a pacing plan, a fueling plan I had practiced, and a 55:00 10K on tired legs two weeks before. The fitness was there. Every prediction said 1:55–1:58 was realistic.

Then race day arrived: 15°C at the start, rising toward 20°C in the second half.

## The Plan

The plan was a controlled negative split (a faster second half):

- **Km 1–3:** 5:45/km — hold back on the downhill and protect the quads
- **Km 4–8:** 5:40/km — settle into a rhythm
- **Km 9–21.1:** 5:35/km — build and hold

Four gels: at km 3, km 7, a gel with caffeine at km 12, and a last one at km 15–16 to cover the exact section where I fell apart last year. Water at every station, with some poured over my head to keep my body temperature down.

## What Happened

The first few kilometers went mostly to plan. 5:37 for km 1, 5:42 for km 2. Then I sped up to 5:20 for km 3. That was not a loss of discipline. The start area was full of runners at 7:00–7:30/km. I had to get past them, or spend the next 5 km weaving through traffic on a steep downhill.

Up to km 14 I was steady, averaging 5:40–5:50. Heart rate under control. Power around 220–245w. Then the heat began to bite.

Km 15: 6:19. Km 16: 6:06. The slowdown was real, and I could feel it. My legs were heavy — not painful, just slow to answer. That annoyed me, so I pushed back to 5:41 at km 17. The heat took its payment at km 20: 6:47.

I finished in 2:06:08.

## Last Year vs. This Year — Same Time, Different Story

Here is why the clock is not telling the truth.

**Last year (7°C, perfect conditions):**
- Started at 5:31/km on the downhill
- Heart rate reached 177 by km 19
- Power fell to 184w
- Km 19: 7:03. Km 20: 7:20. Km 21: 7:06
- I could barely walk afterwards

**This year (15–20°C):**
- Started at 5:37/km — controlled
- Heart rate stayed around 160–173, partly thanks to the water on my head
- Power never dropped below 199w
- My worst kilometer was 6:47, and only once
- I walked away feeling fine

Last year I ran out of fuel completely. My heart rate was at its limit and my muscles had nothing left. This year I slowed down in the heat, but I stayed calm, fueled properly, and finished with something still in the tank that the temperature simply would not let me use.

## The 10K Comparison That Tells the Real Story

Two weeks before this race, I ran a 10K in 55:00 — on legs that had covered an 18 km easy run the day before. It was a controlled negative split, and I finished with a 4:45 last kilometer.

Last April, one week before the 2:06 half, I ran a 10K in 55:31 on fresh legs. I started at 4:55 and slowed to 5:59 twice. It was an uneven, stressful effort.

Same time. Completely different execution. The training block changed the way I race, even if the half marathon clock did not show it.

## What the Heat Costs

Research suggests that for every degree above about 12°C, trained runners lose roughly 1–1.5% of their performance. At 20°C that is a 3–4% loss, which at 1:56 pace is 4–5 minutes.

1:56 + 5 minutes = 2:01. Add the crowded start and some fading on the hills, and 2:06 makes complete sense.

On the course I saw runners collapse and receive help from medical staff. The heat was not a small problem — it was the thing that decided the race. Staying on my feet, finishing strong enough to walk afterwards, and not ending up on a stretcher was the real win, even if it does not feel like one.

## What I'm Taking Forward

Sub-2 is possible. The data says so. The pacing discipline was there. The fueling was there. The mental strength was there too — I fought back at km 17 instead of letting the race fall apart.

What I need is either cooler weather or a bigger engine. I am choosing the bigger engine. My plan for the summer is simple. Stop taking seasons off, raise my weekly distance from 20 km to 40–50 km, and build the kind of aerobic base that makes sub-2 possible in any conditions.

The goal is not to become a runner who can break 2:00 on the perfect day. It is to become a runner for whom 2:00 is never in doubt.

2:06 twice. Same number. A different runner. The next one will be different on the clock too.

posts.content:
# Understanding VDOT and Training Paces

When I ran my first half marathon at BMO Vancouver in 2024, I finished in 3:01:00. I had no idea what pace I was supposed to run in training. I just ran as hard as I could, every single day.

A year later I crossed the same finish line in 2:06:00 — 55 minutes faster. The difference was not only more miles. It was running the *right* pace on the *right* days. And that started when I understood VDOT.

## What is VDOT?

VDOT is a measure of your current running fitness, created by the well-known coach Dr. Jack Daniels. VO2max needs a lab test, but VDOT can be estimated from any recent race result.

The great thing about VDOT is that one number gives you all of your training paces:

- **Easy pace** for recovery runs
- **Marathon pace** for parts of your long runs
- **Threshold pace** for tempo runs
- **Interval pace** for track workouts
- **Repetition pace** for building speed

## Why This Changed Everything for Me

Before I understood pace zones, I ran every run at the same moderate effort. It felt useful, but I was actually damaging my own training.

When I joined a run club in Vancouver, they made me slow down on easy days. I mean runs that felt almost embarrassingly slow. But here is what happened:

1. I stopped feeling tired all the time
2. My speed workouts finally felt fast
3. I could put consistent weeks together without breaking down
4. I stopped staring at my watch during runs

The breakthrough was not running harder. It was **running smarter**.

## How to Find Your VDOT

The easiest way is to use a [pace calculator](/calculator) with a recent race result. Enter your time from a 5K, 10K, half marathon or marathon, and you get your VDOT score straight away.

I built the TrainPace calculator because other tools frustrated me — full of ads, awkward unit conversions, and hidden features. I just wanted my zones without clicking past clickbait.

### Example VDOT Paces

For a runner with a 45:00 10K (VDOT about 45):

| Zone | Pace/Mile | Purpose |
|------|-----------|----------|
| Easy | 9:30-10:00 | Recovery, base building |
| Marathon | 8:15 | Race-specific endurance |
| Threshold | 7:35 | Lactate clearance |
| Interval | 7:00 | VO2max development |
| Repetition | 6:30 | Running economy |

## The Hardest Lesson: Easy Days Are Easy

Most runners — me included — run their easy days too fast. You feel good, so you push the pace. But that leads to:

- Not recovering fully between hard sessions
- Poorer quality on workout days
- Progress that stops, or even goes backwards

My run club taught me that easy pace should be about 2 minutes slower than race pace. The first time I tried it, it felt ridiculous. But that is where your body adapts.

## Adjusting Your VDOT

Your VDOT should rise as you get fitter. Test again every 4-6 weeks with a time trial or a race. As your VDOT goes up, your training paces move with it.

I went from barely finishing a half marathon to aiming for under 2:00. Every feature in TrainPace is something I used to plan my own racing, run it, and improve it.

## Getting Started

Ready to find your training paces? Go to our [Pace Calculator](/calculator) and enter your most recent race time. You will have your own paces in seconds.

Remember: the goal is not to run fast every day. It is to run the *right* pace every day. That is how a 3:01 becomes a 2:06.

posts.content:
# Marathon Fueling: Everything You Need to Know

For my first half marathon at BMO Vancouver, I carried 10 gels and 2 heavy water bottles. I had no idea what I actually needed. I just wanted to prove I could do something hard.

I finished in 3:01:00 and spent the next week barely able to walk down stairs.

A year later I used the fuel planner I had built, and it told me I needed 3 gels. I did not quite trust it, so I took 5. It turned out that 3 would have been enough. Even I did not believe my own math at first.

That is why I am writing this — so you do not make the same mistakes.

## Why Fueling Matters

Your body stores about 2,000 calories of glycogen (stored carbohydrate) in your muscles and liver. A marathon burns about 2,600-3,000 calories. A half marathon burns about 1,300-1,500.

If you take in no fuel during the race, you *will* run out of glycogen. When that happens you "bonk" or "hit the wall" — a sudden, sharp loss of energy that turns a good race into a long walk to the finish.

## Pre-Race Nutrition

### Carb Loading (2-3 Days Before)

Carb loading is not about eating pasta until you feel ill. It means:

- Raising your carbohydrate intake to 8-10 g per kg of body weight
- Eating less fiber, so your stomach stays calm
- Drinking enough water

**Good carb loading foods:**
- White rice and pasta
- Bread, bagels, English muffins
- Potatoes (without the skin)
- Bananas
- Sports drinks

### Race Morning (2-4 Hours Before)

Eat a breakfast you know well, with 100-150 g of carbohydrate:

- Oatmeal with a banana
- A bagel with peanut butter
- Toast with jam

Avoid foods high in fiber or fat, which can upset your stomach.

## During the Race

### The Golden Rules

1. **Start early** - begin fueling at mile 4-5, not when you already feel hungry
2. **Stay consistent** - take fuel every 20-30 minutes
3. **Practice in training** - never try anything new on race day

### How Much to Take

Aim for 30-60 g of carbohydrate per hour. Most gels contain 20-25 g, so that means:

- 1 gel every 20-30 minutes, OR
- The same amount from sports drink, chews or real food

### Gel vs. Chews vs. Drink

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|--------|------|------|
| Gels | Fast absorption, portable | Can upset your stomach |
| Chews | Easier on the stomach, satisfying | You have to chew while running |
| Sports drink | Fuel and hydration together | Heavy to carry |

## Creating Your Fueling Plan

I built the [Fuel Planner](/fuel) because there were no fueling calculators when I was training. How many gels do I really need? I had to work it out myself.

Now you can build your own race-day nutrition plan based on:

- Your target pace
- The race distance
- Where the aid stations are
- The fuel you like

## Common Mistakes

1. **Carrying too much** - like me, with 10 gels. Work out what you need.
2. **Skipping breakfast** - you need those carbohydrates before the start
3. **Starting to fuel too late** - once you feel hungry, it is already too late
4. **Trying new products** - test everything in training first
5. **Forgetting electrolytes** - losing sodium hurts your performance

## What I Do Now

For my 2:06 half marathon I had a plan:
- Gel at km 7
- Gel at km 14
- Water at every aid station

Simple. Practiced. Carried out.

No bonking. No regrets. I crossed the line smiling instead of limping.

## The Bottom Line

Good fueling will not make you faster than your fitness allows, but bad fueling will definitely make you slower. Plan ahead, practice in training, and follow the plan on race day.

Ready to make your plan? Try our [Fuel Planner](/fuel) to get your nutrition right. Do not be the person with 10 gels and 2 bottles, wondering what went wrong.

# How Elevation Affects Your Race Strategy

Before my second BMO Vancouver Half Marathon, I studied the course elevation profile kilometer by kilometer. I knew where the hills were, how steep they were, and exactly how I would change my effort on each one.

That 55-minute improvement was not luck. Part of it was knowing the route before I got there.

## The Cost of Climbing

Running uphill takes much more energy than running on the flat. Research suggests:

- **4% grade**: about 15% more energy used
- **8% grade**: about 30% more energy used
- **Downhills**: they save some energy, but they stress your muscles in a different way

So in terms of effort, a hilly race is really "longer" than a flat one.

## Why I Built the Elevation Finder

The elevation tools I could find frustrated me. I wanted to see the gradient as a percentage and plan my effort, not just look at a fixed chart. Strava hides useful features. Other sites are full of ads.

So I built something that actually helps you understand your course.

## Reading Elevation Profiles

When you study a course, look for:

### Total Elevation Gain

The total number of feet or meters you climb. Boston has about 800 ft of climbing, while Chicago has only about 200 ft. That difference matters.

### Where the Hills Are

The position of the hills matters:

- **Early hills** (miles 1-10): easier to handle on fresh legs
- **Mid-race hills** (miles 10-20): they can break your rhythm
- **Late hills** (miles 20+): the hardest, because your glycogen is low

### How Steep They Are

A short, steep hill feels very different from a long, gentle slope. Know what is coming.

## Pacing Strategies for Hills

### The Effort-Based Approach

Instead of holding your pace, hold your effort:

- **Uphills**: slow down and keep your heart rate steady
- **Downhills**: let gravity help you, but do not brake too much
- **Flat sections**: go back to goal pace

That is what I did at BMO. Controlled effort on the hills. Disciplined pacing in the early kilometers. No panic when my watch showed slower splits on the climbs.

### Time Cost Estimates

Rough guidelines for adjusting your pace:

| Grade | Pace Adjustment |
|-------|----------------|
| 2% up | +15 sec/mile |
| 4% up | +30 sec/mile |
| 2% down | -10 sec/mile |
| 4% down | -15 sec/mile |

## Analyzing Your Race Course

Use our [Elevation Finder](/elevation-finder) to:

1. Upload the GPX file of your course
2. Look at the elevation profile
3. Find the important climbs and descents
4. Plan your strategy section by section

## Training for Hills

If your goal race is hilly, your training should include:

- **Hill repeats**: to build strength and climb more efficiently
- **Long runs with hills**: to copy race conditions
- **Downhill practice**: to protect your quads and learn to run down under control

## Major Marathon Elevation Profiles

We have detailed breakdowns for the major marathons:

- [Boston Marathon](/preview-route/boston) - the famous Newton Hills
- [New York City Marathon](/preview-route/nyc) - five bridges and rolling ground
- [Chicago Marathon](/preview-route/chicago) - completely flat and fast
- [Berlin Marathon](/preview-route/berlin) - a flat course for personal bests

## The Mental Game

Hills are as much mental as physical. These strategies help:

- **Break the hill into parts** - focus on reaching the next tree or corner
- **Use a short phrase** - "smooth and steady" or "relax and float"
- **Look ahead, not down** - keep your body upright
- **Welcome the challenge** - hills are where races are won

## Key Takeaways

1. Respect the elevation. It will cost you time and energy.
2. Adjust your pace by effort, not only by the numbers
3. Know your course before race day
4. Train for the ground you will actually run on

Upload your race course to our [Elevation Finder](/elevation-finder) and start planning your strategy today. Knowing the course is half the job.

posts.content:
# First Half or Marathon? What I Wish I Knew

As a kid, I could not run 6 laps in under 15 minutes in gym class. Running was not something I did.

Then, in May 2024, I crossed the finish line of the BMO Vancouver Half Marathon in 3:01:00. I survived, but only just. The following week was awful — sore, in pain, unable to walk down stairs without a grimace.

But finishing gave me something I did not know I needed: proof that I could get through hard things.

Here is what I wish someone had told me before that first race.

## 1. The Long Run Is King

Your weekly long run is the most important session of the week. It builds:

- Endurance
- Mental strength
- Confidence
- Your ability to burn fat as fuel

Do not skip long runs. Do not rush them. Run them at conversational pace.

## 2. Easy Days Must Be Easy

This was the hardest lesson. When I joined a run club, they made me slow down on easy days — runs that felt almost embarrassingly slow at the time.

But that is where my body adapted.

Easy pace should be about 2 minutes slower than race pace. If you cannot hold a full conversation, slow down.

Use our [Pace Calculator](/calculator) to find your correct easy pace.

## 3. Consistency Beats Intensity

Four 40-minute runs a week beat one 3-hour hero session. Your body adapts to regular stress, not to occasional huge efforts.

I trained consistently for 24 weeks before my second half marathon. That consistency — not any single workout — is what took 55 minutes off my time.

## 4. Rest Is Training

Your body adapts during recovery, not during the workout. Sleep 7-9 hours. Take rest days seriously. Your body will thank you on race day.

## 5. Nothing New on Race Day

This golden rule covers:

- Shoes
- Clothing
- Fuel (gels, drinks)
- Breakfast
- Your routine before the start

I took 10 gels and 2 heavy bottles to my first race because I had no idea what I really needed. Test everything in training.

## 6. Start Slower Than You Think

The first few miles will feel easy. You will want to put time in the bank. Do not do it.

Start 10-15 seconds slower than goal pace. You can always speed up later. You cannot get those early miles back.

## 7. Fuel Early and Often

Do not wait until you feel hungry. By then it is too late.

Start taking gels or other fuel by km 6-8, and carry on every 20-30 minutes. Have a look at our [Fuel Planner](/fuel) to build your plan.

## 8. Expect the Hard Part (But Plan Around It)

Km 15-18 of a half marathon will be hard. Really hard. That is normal. It happens to everyone.

A plan helps:
- Break the race into sections
- Have a few short phrases ready to repeat
- Remember that the bad patch will pass

## 9. Enjoy the Experience

Your first long race only happens once. Look around. Read the signs. High-five the kids. This is a celebration.

## 10. Finishing Is the Goal

Forget time goals for your first race. Really.

The goal is to cross the finish line healthy and happy. Everything else is a bonus.

A year after my 3:01, I crossed the line in 2:06 — smiling instead of limping. But that first finish, painful as it was, proved to the kid inside me that hard things are possible.

---

Ready to start? Get your [training paces](/calculator), study your [race course](/elevation-finder), and plan your [fueling strategy](/fuel).

You can do this.

author.name: Alex
author.bio: Developer & runner. Went from 3:01 to 2:06 in the half marathon.

posts.content:
# Recovery Strategies That Actually Work

During my 24-week training block for BMO Vancouver, I had knee pain that would not go away. It probably came from skipping strength training — a mistake I will not make again.

Training breaks you down. Recovery builds you back up, stronger. Here is what I learned about recovering more intelligently.

## Why Recovery Matters

Your body adapts while you rest, not while you run. When you run:

- Muscle fibers get tiny tears
- Your glycogen (stored carbohydrate) runs down
- Inflammation goes up
- Your hormones move up and down

Recovery repairs this damage and makes you stronger. Skip it and you stop improving — or, like me, you get injured.

## The Big Three: Sleep, Nutrition, Easy Days

### 1. Sleep (The Number One Recovery Tool)

No supplement, gadget or ice bath comes close to sleep:

- **7-9 hours** is the target for most runners
- **Growth hormone** is highest during deep sleep
- **Your brain stores what it has learned**, which helps your movement skills
- **Your immune system** repairs itself while you rest

**Sleep tips for runners:**
- Keep the same schedule every day
- Cool, dark room (65-68°F / 18-20°C)
- No screens for an hour before bed
- No caffeine after 2pm

### 2. Post-Run Nutrition

The 30-60 minutes after a run is the best time to start recovering:

- **Protein**: 20-30 g to repair muscle (whey, Greek yogurt, eggs)
- **Carbohydrate**: to refill glycogen (banana, rice, oats)
- **Ratio**: 3:1 or 4:1 carbohydrate to protein

**Quick recovery snacks:**
- Chocolate milk (seriously, it works)
- Banana and peanut butter
- Greek yogurt with granola
- A protein smoothie

### 3. Easy Days Are Easy

This is where most runners go wrong. I know, because I was one of them.

My run club in Vancouver made me slow down. Easy runs should be:

- **Conversational** - you can talk in full sentences
- **About 2 minutes slower** than race pace
- **Low heart rate** - what people call zone 2

Use our [Pace Calculator](/calculator) to find your correct easy pace. Running too fast on easy days is the number one cause of overtraining.

## Active Recovery Methods

### Walking

The most underrated recovery tool:
- Moves blood around your body without adding stress
- 20-30 minutes on rest days
- Good for your head as well as your legs

### Foam Rolling

Research shows moderate benefits for:
- Reducing muscle soreness
- Improving flexibility in the short term
- **Best time**: after a run, or before bed

### Stretching

- **Dynamic stretching** (moving stretches): before runs
- **Static stretching** (held stretches): after runs, or in a separate session
- Hold each stretch for 30-60 seconds

## Recovery Week (Deload)

Every 3-4 weeks, cut your training volume by 20-30%:

- Fewer miles or kilometers
- The same intensity in your key workouts
- More sleep
- Focus on form, not fitness

This prevents overtraining and lets your body absorb the work more deeply.

## Warning Signs of Under-Recovery

Watch for these warning signs:

- Tiredness that does not go away
- A higher resting heart rate
- Poor sleep
- Bad mood or short temper
- Worse performance
- Getting ill often
- Losing motivation

If you notice several of these, take extra rest days. I wish I had listened to these signals earlier, before my knee got worse.

## The Bottom Line

Recovery is not laziness — it is strategy. The runners who recover best can train the hardest. Protect your sleep, eat well, and respect your easy days.

Your next personal best is built on rest days. Trust me. I learned this one the hard way.

author.bio: Developer & runner. Went from 3:01 to 2:06 in the half marathon.

posts.content:
# Tempo Runs: The Workout That Made Me Faster

My 24-week training plan had one simple structure:
- 1 long run per week
- 1 speed workout per week
- Easy runs 2 minutes slower than race pace

That speed workout was usually a tempo run. Here is why they work and how to do them properly.

## What Is a Tempo Run?

A tempo run is a steady effort at a "comfortably hard" pace — faster than easy running, slower than racing. The aim is to run at or near your **lactate threshold**: the pace where your body clears lactate as fast as it produces it.

**How it feels**: you can say short phrases, but not full sentences. It is demanding, but you can keep it going.

## Why Tempo Runs Work

At threshold pace you train your body to:

1. **Clear lactate better** - so the moment when you fall apart comes later
2. **Run more efficiently** - use less energy at faster paces
3. **Build mental strength** - practice staying calm while it hurts
4. **Get race-ready** - half marathon pace is close to threshold pace

## Finding Your Tempo Pace

There are several ways to find it:

### Method 1: Race Prediction

Use our [Pace Calculator](/calculator) with a recent race time. Your threshold pace is usually:

- About 25-30 seconds per km slower than 10K pace
- About 15-20 seconds per km faster than half marathon pace

### Method 2: Heart Rate

85-90% of your maximum heart rate.

### Method 3: How It Feels

An effort of 6-7 out of 10. "Comfortably hard." You want to slow down, but you do not have to.

## Tempo Run Formats

### Classic Tempo (20-40 minutes)

The standard version:
- 10-15 min easy warm-up
- 20-40 min at tempo pace
- 10 min easy cool-down

**Best for**: general threshold work and half marathon training

### Cruise Intervals

The tempo is broken into pieces with short recoveries:
- 3-4 x 10 minutes at tempo with a 2 min jog
- 5 x 6 minutes at tempo with a 90 sec jog

**Best for**: your first weeks of tempo training, and longer threshold sessions

### Progression Tempo

Start slower, finish faster:
- First third at marathon pace
- Second third at tempo pace
- Last third at 10K effort

**Best for**: learning to finish races strongly

## Common Tempo Mistakes

### 1. Running Too Fast

The most common error. If you are racing your tempo run, you have missed the point. It should feel controlled.

### 2. Running Too Long

More is not always better. 40 minutes of good tempo running beats 60 minutes of messy threshold running.

### 3. Skipping the Warm-Up

You need 10-15 minutes of easy running before you start tempo pace. Cold muscles do not respond well.

## Sample Week with Tempo

| Day | Workout |
|-----|----------|
| Monday | Rest or cross-train |
| Tuesday | Easy run |
| Wednesday | **Tempo: 15 min warmup + 25 min tempo + 10 min cooldown** |
| Thursday | Easy run |
| Friday | Rest |
| Saturday | Long run |
| Sunday | Easy run |

This is close to what I did for 24 weeks. Simple, manageable, effective.

## The Mental Game

Tempo runs teach you to be comfortable while you are uncomfortable. That carries straight over into racing:

- You learn what "hard but sustainable" feels like
- You practice staying calm when it gets tough
- You build confidence in your own fitness

By race day I knew exactly what tempo effort felt like. I trusted my legs because I had done the work.

## Key Takeaways

1. Tempo = threshold pace = comfortably hard
2. Use the [Pace Calculator](/calculator) to find your tempo pace
3. Start with 20 minutes and build up slowly
4. Do not race your tempo runs — control is everything
5. One tempo run a week is plenty for most runners

Regular tempo work will make you a faster and more confident racer. Trust the process.

posts.content:
# How to Choose the Right Running Shoes

With hundreds of models and endless marketing claims, choosing running shoes can feel confusing. Here is what actually matters.

## The Truth About Running Shoes

Let us start with what the research tells us:

1. **Comfort matters most** - the best sign that a shoe will keep you injury-free is that it feels comfortable
2. **Expensive is not always better** - the price of a shoe has no clear link to injury rates
3. **Pronation control is overrated** - motion control shoes do not prevent injuries for most runners
4. **Rotating shoes helps** - using several pairs lowers your injury risk

## Key Factors to Consider

### 1. Fit

The most important factor:

- **Toe box**: enough room to move your toes
- **Heel**: close-fitting but not tight, with no slipping
- **Width**: choose a wider or narrower version if you need one
- **Length**: about a thumb's width between your longest toe and the front

**Pro tip**: shop in the afternoon, when your feet are slightly swollen.

### 2. Cushioning (Stack Height)

How much foam sits between you and the ground:

| Level | Stack Height | Best For |
|-------|--------------|----------|
| Minimal | 0-15mm | Experienced runners, speed work |
| Low | 15-25mm | Tempo runs, shorter races |
| Medium | 25-35mm | Daily training, versatile |
| Max | 35mm+ | Long runs, recovery, high mileage |

### 3. Drop (Heel-to-Toe Offset)

The height difference between the heel and the front of the shoe:

- **High drop (10-12mm)**: traditional, good if you land on your heel
- **Medium drop (6-8mm)**: balanced and flexible
- **Low drop (0-4mm)**: encourages a midfoot landing, and your body needs time to get used to it

**Warning**: do not switch suddenly to low drop shoes. Change slowly.

### 4. Weight

- **Daily trainers**: 255-310g (9-11 oz)
- **Tempo/race shoes**: 200-255g (7-9 oz)
- **Super shoes (carbon plate)**: 170-230g (6-8 oz)

Lighter shoes are faster, but they protect you less.

## Types of Running Shoes

### Daily Trainers

The shoe you use for most of your miles:
- Long-lasting
- Comfortable
- Medium cushioning
- Lasts 500-800 km

**Examples**: Nike Pegasus, Brooks Ghost, ASICS Cumulus, New Balance 880

### Tempo/Uptempo Shoes

For faster workouts and shorter races:
- Lighter
- More responsive
- Less cushioning
- Lasts 300-600 km

### Racing Flats/Super Shoes

For races and key workouts:
- Carbon fiber plates
- Maximum energy return
- Very light
- Lasts 150-300 km

## Building a Shoe Rotation

Research shows that rotating shoes cuts injury risk by about 39%. A good rotation:

1. **Daily trainer** (60% of your miles)
2. **Uptempo shoe** (25% of your miles)
3. **Easy day or recovery shoe** (15% of your miles)

You can add a racing shoe as well if you compete.

## When to Replace Shoes

Signs that your shoes are finished:

- **Flat midsole** - the foam no longer springs back
- **Worn sole** - clear wear on the bottom of the shoe
- **New aches** - unusual soreness after runs
- **Distance** - 500-800 km for most trainers

Keep a note of the distance in your training log.

## Carbon Plate Shoes: Worth It?

The super shoe revolution is real:

**Pros:**
- Research shows 2-4% energy savings
- You can feel the spring and the efficiency
- Legal in all races

**Cons:**
- Expensive ($200-300 CAD)
- They do not last long
- They can hide fatigue, which raises your injury risk if you use them too often

**Best practice**: save them for races and key workouts. Do not train in them every day.

## The Bottom Line

1. **Put comfort first** - if it feels wrong, it is wrong
2. **Get properly fitted** - visit a specialty running store
3. **Rotate your shoes** - several pairs lower your injury risk
4. **Replace them regularly** - worn-out shoes cause problems
5. **Do not overthink it** - the best shoe is the one you will actually run in

Once you have the right shoes, focus on training well. Use our [Pace Calculator](/calculator) to get your training paces right.

author.name: Alex
author.bio: Developer & runner. Went from 3:01 to 2:06 in the half marathon.

posts.content:
# Half Marathon Pacing: How I Ran 55 Minutes Faster

My first BMO Vancouver Half Marathon: 3:01:00. I had no pacing plan. I just ran until I could not run any more.

My second BMO Vancouver Half Marathon: 2:06:00. I ran the race exactly as planned. Controlled effort on the hills. Disciplined pacing in the early kilometers. Fuel taken on schedule.

Here is the pacing strategy that made the difference.

## The Half Marathon Challenge

At 21.1 km, the half marathon sits in an unusual place:

- **Too long** to run on adrenaline alone
- **Too short** to recover from an early mistake
- **Fast enough** to hurt from start to finish

That makes pacing crucial. Get it wrong and you will suffer, as I did the first time. Get it right and you will fly.

## Pacing Strategies

### 1. Even Splits (What I Did)

Run every kilometer at the same pace:

**Pros:**
- It is the most efficient way for your body to work
- It is predictable and easy to control
- Consistency builds confidence

**How to do it:**
- Know your goal pace exactly (use our [Pace Calculator](/calculator))
- Check your split at every kilometer
- The first 5K should feel almost too easy

I aimed for 6:00/km. The first few kilometers felt slow. But I trusted the plan.

### 2. Slight Negative Split

Run the second half 30-60 seconds faster:

**How to do it:**
- First half: 10-15 seconds/km slower than goal pace
- Km 12-16: settle into goal pace
- Last 5K: give it everything

### 3. Controlled Positive Split

Plan to slow down slightly in the second half:

**When it works:**
- Hot weather
- Hilly courses
- When you are chasing a very ambitious personal best

## The First Kilometer Trap

Km 1 always feels easy. The adrenaline is high, the crowd is cheering, and your legs are fresh.

**The problem**: starting too fast leads to a painful second half.

**The solution**:
- Run km 1 10-15 seconds slower than goal pace
- Let faster runners go past (you will catch them later)
- Hold yourself back on purpose

I let people pass me at the start. I caught most of them by km 15.

## The Middle Kilometers (10-16)

This is the empty middle part of the half marathon:

- The excitement has gone
- The finish is still a long way off
- Your pace can slip without you noticing

**How to stay on pace:**
- Break it into 2-3 km pieces
- Focus on your form and your breathing
- Find a pacer or a group running your speed
- Use buildings or corners as small targets

## The Final 5K

Km 17-21 are where races are won or lost:

- Reach for your mental reserves
- Repeat a short phrase ("strong and steady", "I trained for this")
- Catch the runners ahead of you
- Shorten your stride if you are struggling

This is what you trained for. The discomfort will not last.

## Race-Day Execution Checklist

### Before the Race:
- [ ] Know your goal pace per km
- [ ] Know the course (hills, turns, aid stations)
- [ ] Set your watch to show your current pace
- [ ] Have your fueling plan ready

### During the Race:
- [ ] Start carefully
- [ ] Check your pace at each km marker
- [ ] Take fuel at the planned times
- [ ] Stay calm if you are off pace

### Mental Cues:
- Km 1-7: "easy, controlled, relaxed"
- Km 8-15: "smooth, steady, patient"
- Km 16-21: "strong, focused, finish"

## Adjusting for Conditions

### Hilly Course

This was the key at BMO. I studied the course in advance with [Elevation Finder](/elevation-finder):
- Adjust your effort on hills, not your pace
- Do not speed up too much on the downhills
- Accept slower splits on the climbs and faster ones on the descents

### Hot Weather
- Slow your goal pace by 1-2% for every 10°C above 15°C
- Start even more carefully than usual
- Pay attention to fluids and electrolytes

## The Bottom Line

The half marathon rewards patience and punishes over-confidence. Trust your fitness, start carefully, and race the second half.

That 55-minute improvement was not luck. It was data, consistency, and following a plan.

Put your goal time into our [Pace Calculator](/calculator) to get your km splits, check your course on [Elevation Finder](/elevation-finder), and plan your [fueling strategy](/fuel).

Then go and do it.
