author.bio: Developer & runner. Went from 3:01 to 2:06 in the half marathon.

posts.content:
# How to Break Through a Running Plateau

I ran the same half marathon time three years in a row.

Not roughly the same — within two minutes of the same time, three years running, even though I trained consistently and worked harder in every cycle.

Then I made a few specific changes and took 12 minutes off the following year.

A running plateau is not a limit on your talent. It is a sign that something in your training needs to change. Here is how to find out what.

## What a Plateau Actually Is

A plateau happens when your training keeps asking your body for changes it has already made. Your aerobic system has adapted to your current training load, so more of the same brings no new response.

This is different from being undertrained (not running enough) or overtrained (running too much without recovery). A plateau is a problem of precision: the volume and intensity that built your current fitness are not enough to build the next level of fitness.

The answer is not to train harder. It is to train differently.

## The Most Common Causes

### 1. All Your Runs Are the Same Pace

This is the most common cause of a plateau in recreational runners. Every run is a medium effort — not easy enough to be truly aerobic, not hard enough to force new adaptations.

The fix is to split your training into two clear groups. 80% of your runs should be genuinely easy (conversational pace, well below your lactate threshold). 20% should be properly hard (tempo runs, intervals). The medium-pace running that most recreational runners fall into gives you neither the aerobic base of easy running nor the threshold gains of hard running.

Use the [VDOT Calculator](/vdot) to get your real training paces. Most runners are surprised at how slow their easy pace should be.

### 2. No Structured Speed Work

If you have been running for more than a year without structured tempo runs or intervals, you are leaving improvement on the table.

Easy running builds your aerobic base, but it cannot do the whole job. It does not push your lactate threshold or your VO2max ceiling. Adding one quality session a week (a 20-minute tempo run, or 5 × 800m intervals) is often enough to start the improvement again.

Be patient: the first 3-4 sessions will feel rough. By session 6-8, the pace starts to feel manageable.

### 3. Not Enough Mileage for Your Goals

Every race distance has a minimum useful mileage range. If you run 30 km a week and you want a sub-3:30 marathon, you are not running enough for that goal. Marathon performance is built on sustained mileage, not on quality sessions alone.

A rough guide:
- 5K PR goal: 40-50km per week
- 10K PR goal: 50-65km per week
- Half marathon PR goal: 60-80km per week
- Marathon PR goal: 70-100km per week

These are averages, not rules. But if you are 30-40% below these ranges, mileage is probably what is holding you back.

### 4. No Phases in Your Training

Repeating the same training week for ever does not work. Your body needs a planned cycle of stress and recovery in order to adapt.

Training in phases means:
- Base phase (easy volume, no hard quality work)
- Development phase (quality work comes in)
- Sharpening phase (race-specific intensity)
- Taper and race

If you do not organize your training into phases, and every week looks much the same, your body gets used to the constant load and stops improving.

### 5. Not Enough Recovery

Sometimes a plateau is not caused by too little training. It is caused by too little recovery. Your body adapts during rest, not during the run. If you are always slightly tired, you never actually absorb the training.

Signs: your easy runs feel hard, your resting heart rate is higher than usual, you are not looking forward to training, and your sleep is poor.

The fix: a deliberate recovery week every 3-4 weeks (cut your volume by 30-40% and keep the easy running), and take your rest days seriously.

## How to Diagnose Your Plateau

Ask yourself these questions:

1. Do I have genuinely easy days and genuinely hard days, or is everything medium?
2. Have I done any structured quality work (tempo runs, intervals) in the last 8 weeks?
3. Is my weekly mileage right for my goal race?
4. Have I raced or run a time trial recently to check my current VDOT?
5. Am I recovering well (good sleep, no constant tiredness)?

Usually one of these stands out. Fix that one first.

## Getting Your Numbers Right Again

Before you change your training, find out where you actually are. A tune-up race or time trial (a 5K or 10K at full effort) gives you your current VDOT and updates your training paces.

Many runners are using paces based on a race from 12-18 months ago. If your fitness has changed, in either direction, training at old paces means every session is set wrongly.

Update your VDOT after every goal race, and ideally run a tune-up race halfway through a training cycle to check that you are training at the right intensities.

## Be Patient With the New Training

When you change your training to break a plateau, the results take time. The aerobic gains from extra easy mileage show up in 6-8 weeks. Lactate threshold gains from tempo work take 4-6 weeks. VO2max gains from intervals take 4-8 weeks.

If you change your training in week 1 and expect a personal best in week 4, you will be disappointed and decide it did not work.

Give the new training 8-12 weeks before you judge it. Most plateaus that are diagnosed correctly and treated with patience are broken within one training cycle.

posts.title: Overtraining: The Signs I Ignored (Until I Burned Out)
posts.excerpt: Overtraining does not announce itself. It builds over weeks of feeling slightly wrong — slow runs, poor sleep, a short temper — until one day you cannot run.

author.name: Alex
author.bio: Developer & runner. Went from 3:01 to 2:06 in the half marathon.

posts.content:
# Overtraining: The Signs I Ignored (Until I Burned Out)

Six weeks before my goal marathon, I could not finish a 5-kilometer easy run.

I had been training for 20 weeks. The mileage looked right. The workouts were hitting the numbers. But I felt empty — heavy legs, hard breathing at a pace I should hardly have noticed, and a complete lack of motivation that I kept explaining away as pre-race nerves.

It was not nerves. It was overtraining syndrome.

I withdrew from the race. Recovery took eight weeks. Here is what I missed.

## What Overtraining Actually Is

Overtraining syndrome (OTS) is a medical condition caused by too much training without enough recovery. It is not the same as normal tiredness, which goes away after a few rest days, or short-term overreaching, which clears in 1-2 weeks of easier training.

Real OTS can take weeks or months to clear. The hormonal problems behind it — high cortisol, low testosterone, and a stress system that will not switch off — do not correct themselves overnight.

The key point: you cannot train your way out of OTS. The only treatment is rest.

## Early Warning Signs (That I Ignored)

Most runners who develop OTS can look back and find the signs 3-6 weeks before the crisis. On their own, the signs look small. Together, they form a clear pattern.

**Performance stops improving, or gets worse.** Workouts that should be manageable feel hard. Interval pace feels harder than your training log says it should. You start a tempo run at target pace and cannot hold it.

I called this "tired legs" and pushed on.

**A higher resting heart rate.** A resting heart rate 5-7 beats per minute above your normal level for several mornings in a row is a reliable early warning. If you wear a smartwatch, the data is already there.

I noticed it but did not track it properly.

**Poor sleep.** Trouble falling asleep or staying asleep, even though you are physically tired. That is the stress hormone at work: your nervous system stays switched on even when your body wants to rest.

I thought I was anxious about the race.

**Mood changes.** Short temper, no enthusiasm for running, and trouble concentrating. Running should improve your mood, and the runner's high is real. If your runs leave you flat or irritated, something is wrong.

I thought I was stressed about work.

**Soreness that will not go away.** Some soreness is normal. Soreness that does not clear between runs, and is still there three days after a workout, means you are not recovering.

I put this down to "training hard".

## What Causes It

Overtraining is a mismatch between your training load and your ability to recover. The usual causes are:

**Increasing mileage too fast.** The standard guideline is no more than a 10% increase per week. Breaking that rule, especially while keeping the intensity high, overwhelms your body's ability to repair itself.

**Not enough easy days.** Hard sessions need genuinely easy recovery days, not "slightly less hard" days. If your easy pace is still within 15% of your threshold pace, it is not really easy.

**Stress outside running.** Lack of sleep, big life events and illness all reduce your ability to recover. A training load that is fine in a calm period can tip you into overtraining in a stressful one.

**A taper that never happens.** Some runners resist cutting their volume during the taper because it feels like falling behind. But the taper is a planned drop in load, and your body absorbs your training during that time. Skipping it often means arriving at the start line already tired.

## How to Recover

If you catch OTS early — performance has stalled, your heart rate is up, your mood has changed a little — the plan is simple:

1. **Cut your volume by 40-50% for 2 weeks.** Not the intensity, the volume. Keep some structured running, just much less of it.
2. **Protect your sleep.** 8-9 hours a night as a minimum. That is where recovery happens.
3. **Eat enough.** Eating too little while training hard makes OTS come faster. Do not cut calories during a high-mileage block.
4. **Check again after 2 weeks.** If your performance is coming back and you want to run again, build up slowly.

Full OTS is different. If you cannot run without feeling terrible, your mood is badly affected and your motivation has gone, recovery takes longer: 4-8 weeks with very little structured running, or none at all.

## Building the Guard Rails

The best prevention is regular, structured monitoring:

**Track your resting heart rate every day.** Three days in a row of 5 or more beats above your normal level is your early warning. Use it.

**Score every run from 1 to 5 for how hard it felt compared with how hard it should have felt.** If your easy run keeps feeling like a 4 when it should feel like a 2, look into it.

**Put recovery weeks in your plan.** Every 3-4 weeks, cut your volume by 30-40%. Every serious training plan includes this for a reason. Use it.

**Know the difference between training hard and overtraining.** Training hard makes you tired, and that tiredness clears after 24-48 hours of rest. Overtraining makes you tired in a way that does not clear, however much you rest.

The aim of training is to be tired enough to adapt and rested enough to absorb those adaptations. OTS happens when you get the first half right and ignore the second half completely.
